subject: History
title: The World at War (1914–1991)
learningOutcomes: Analyse the major causes of the First World War (Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism).
Explain the role and impact of Indians in WWI, the Lucknow Pact of 1916, and the European mandates in the Middle East.
Describe the causes, main events, end and impact of the Second World War.
Explain the aims, organs and functions of the League of Nations and the United Nations.
Outline the Cold War and its end, and the making of the State of Israel.
Place the key events of 1914–1991 in the correct chronological order.

sections.heading: First World War (1914–1918): Background & Groups
sections.body: The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918 and was triggered by the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austrian throne, by a Serbian nationalist. Germany was the first to declare war. The two sides were the Central Powers (Germany, Austro-Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire) and the Allies (Great Britain, France, Russia, Italy and Japan, with the USA joining from 1917).

sections.heading: Causes of World War I (M.A.I.N.)
sections.body: Four main causes are remembered by the acronym MAIN — Militarism (building up large armies and weapons), Alliances (agreements to defend one another), Imperialism (competing to colonise foreign lands), and Nationalism (the desire of peoples for their own states). The Industrial Revolution fuelled rivalry over markets and raw materials, while the ideas of the French Revolution spread nationalism across Europe.

sections.heading: European Mandates in the Middle East
sections.body: During WWI the secret Sykes-Picot agreement of 1916 planned to divide Ottoman lands. Under the resulting mandate system, the British gained Palestine and Iraq while the French controlled Syria and Lebanon. The League of Nations approved the British mandate over Palestine in 1922.

sections.heading: The Role & Impact of Indians in World War I
sections.body: More than a million Indians were enlisted in the British army and fought in Europe and Mesopotamia; India also supplied animals, materials and a large loan. In return Indians hoped for greater self-rule. In 1916 the Lucknow Pact between the Congress and the Muslim League marked the peak of Hindu-Muslim unity, while the Defense of India Act (1915) was used to repress discontent.

sections.heading: Effects of WWI & the Treaty of Versailles
sections.body: WWI introduced tanks, aircraft, submarines, trench warfare and — after Germany used chlorine gas in 1915 — chemical warfare, killing around eight million soldiers. It ended on 11 November 1918. The harsh Treaty of Versailles (1919) punished Germany, and the German, Russian, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires collapsed.

sections.heading: The League of Nations
sections.body: After WWI the League of Nations was set up to prevent future wars and to tackle problems such as slavery, opium smuggling and refugees. It could not stop the Second World War and was dissolved in 1946, but it paved the way for the United Nations.

sections.heading: Second World War (1939–1945) & Its Causes
sections.body: The Second World War (1939–1945) grew out of unresolved WWI issues, the rise of fascism under leaders like Hitler (Germany), Mussolini (Italy) and Franco (Spain), the Great Depression (1929–1939), and the failed policy of appeasement. The German invasion of Poland led Britain and France to declare war, and Japan's attack on Pearl Harbour on 7 December 1941 brought in the USA. The Axis (Germany, Italy, Japan) fought the Allies (Britain, France, USA, USSR, China).

sections.heading: End & Impact of World War II
sections.body: Winston Churchill announced the end of the war in Europe on 8 May 1945 after Hitler's death. In August 1945 the USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the Japanese Emperor surrendered on 2 September 1945. It was the deadliest war in history; Germany was split into East and West, Korea into North and South, and the USSR took control of several eastern European states.

sections.heading: The Making of the State of Israel
sections.body: Palestine, sacred to Muslims, Jews and Christians, was ruled by the Ottomans from 1517 to 1917. The Balfour Declaration (1917) backed a Jewish homeland; after the Holocaust the UN approved partition in 1947 and Israel declared independence in May 1948, recognised by US President Truman. Pakistan did not recognise Israel.

sections.heading: The United Nations & Its Organs
sections.body: The United Nations was formed on 24 October 1945 in San Francisco by 51 founding countries and now has 193 members. Its six main organs are the General Assembly, the Security Council (five permanent members with veto power), the Economic and Social Council (54 members), the Trusteeship Council, the International Court of Justice (15 judges) and the Secretariat, with headquarters in New York.

sections.heading: The Cold War (1946–1991)
sections.body: The Cold War (1946–1991) was a non-conventional rivalry between the capitalist USA and the communist USSR, begun under the Truman Doctrine. The world split into Western, Eastern and non-aligned groups, and the powers fought proxy wars while technology advanced rapidly. The Berlin Wall was demolished in 1989–1990 and the USSR broke up in 1991, ending the Cold War.

examTips: Remember the causes of WWI with the acronym MAIN: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism.
Central Powers = Germany, Austro-Hungary, Bulgaria, Ottoman Empire. WWI Allies = Britain, France, Russia, Italy, Japan (USA from 1917).
Axis (WWII) = Germany, Italy, Japan. Allies (WWII) = Britain, France, USA, USSR, China.
Key dates: WWI 1914–1918; Treaty of Versailles 1919; WWII 1939–1945; UN formed 24 Oct 1945; Israel 1948; Cold War 1946–1991.
The Lucknow Pact (1916) marked the peak of Hindu-Muslim unity.
The League of Nations failed and was dissolved in 1946; the UN replaced it.
The Cold War was 'cold' because it was not a direct (conventional) war between the USA and USSR.
